articles.title: He taught film dance for a living, then taught himself keyboard, guitar and drums
articles.deck: Ricky Biswasi led an orchestra in Jeypore singing film songs. He talks about the year his friends left, the verse that stopped him, and why he no longer thinks of prayer as asking.

hero.alt: Ricky Biswasi playing a Korg keyboard during a service, with the congregation and a lit cross behind him

interviewMeta.subject: Ricky Biswasi
interviewMeta.subjectBio: A worship leader in Jeypore, Odisha, who leads the Elohim Worship Team and teaches keyboard, guitar and drums to young people in his church. Entirely self-taught.

archiveMeta.editNote: First published as Talent Search #6. Reading order repaired and typographical errors corrected; his answers are otherwise as he gave them.

body.v: Ricky Biswasi leads worship in Jeypore, in southern Odisha. The thing that struck us most about him is that nobody taught him. He worked out the keyboard, then the guitar, then the drums, and he now teaches all three to the young people in his church.
Before that he was known locally for something else. He was a choreographer, and he ran an orchestra team performing film songs on stage.
“I was born into a Christian family”
5Talents: Hello Ricky. Greetings from 5Talents — how are you?
I am doing well by the grace of God. Thank you.
5Talents: When and how did you come to faith in Christ?

I was born and brought up in a Christian family, and although I knew about Jesus Christ from childhood I did not accept Him as my personal saviour until a certain point. As I grew up I became argumentative, covetous, and unfriendly towards nearly everyone in the community I lived in.

Samson's weakness was his anger, and God still turned his negative actions to positive ends. God shaped my life in a similar way, speaking to me through His word and in prayer. As I kept meditating on it, the Holy Spirit taught me to build a better attitude towards other people. One day I accepted Jesus Christ as my personal saviour and my Lord, and I have followed Him since.
Working it out
5Talents: Tell us about the talents you have received.

I believe talents are a gift from God. I have been a dancer since childhood, and I used to teach boys and girls to dance to film songs. After I accepted Jesus I stopped teaching film dance and began teaching dance to the young people in the church instead, and started a worship team.

There was a keyboard in my church and it drew me. I started playing it with no knowledge of chords or combinations at all. God helped me to understand it in stages, and my father taught me some basics. By practising regularly I learned the keyboard, and then I started on the guitar. Later I learned the drums as well.

God has enabled me to lead the Sunday worship service and the youth service, to preach, and to testify to what He has done in my life among young people. He has given me the privilege of teaching them keyboard, guitar and drums.
The verse that ended the orchestra
5Talents: When did you know you wanted to be a worship leader?

In 1999 I was leading an orchestra team, singing secular songs and doing stage programmes. After a while I grew tired of it, and I came to understand that I should not be using my talent the way I had been.
Even everyone that is called by my name: for I have created him for my glory, I have formed him; yea, I have made him.
body.attr: Isaiah 43:7, the verse Ricky read in 1999
body.highlight: I have created him for my glory

body.v: When I read that verse I resolved to leave everything and live my whole life for what I am made for.

That same year I watched some Hillsong worship videos and was moved by them. I wanted a team like that in our church. So I began learning music and studying the word, so that one day such a team could be established here. Later I got the chance to go to Hyderabad, where I led worship and learned new songs in a church for a year, and then I came back and continued with my team, the Elohim Worship Team. The church appointed me as a worship leader.
“Worship is a lifestyle”
5Talents: What does a lifestyle of worship mean to you?

Worship is not only singing and dancing and modern looks. It is presenting our bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God. God has forgiven us so that we can forgive others. When a worshipper talks, everyone should sense the presence of God, and when people look at our faces they should see Jesus rather than us.

As John the Baptist said, He must increase and I must decrease. That is the life of a worshipper — not I, but Christ. And the second thing is to love your neighbour. We should be an example to the world by helping those in need, as Christ did.
“I never felt that I should ask”
5Talents: How would you describe your prayer life?

God is faithful in everything and in every situation. He provides for me abundantly before I ask or even think, so I have never felt that I should ask for anything. Prayer usually means asking for something. I close my eyes and praise and give thanks to God each time, and that habit is my prayer.

My friends left me in 2002 and I was alone, and I started the habit of prayer that year. Every day I sit down in front of my best friend and tell Him everything. That is my prayer life. He gives me whatever I have in mind before I ask for it. So I have only one job now, which is to praise Him and to thank Him.
Writing songs
5Talents: How has Christ inspired your songwriting?

In class eight I wrote a song in a sad frame of mind, and it was not about God, it was about myself — all my feelings and my thoughts about my life. That was my first composition. But after my matriculation, when I started meditating on God's word, I found that what I thought about my life was completely different from how it looks to our Father.

I realised there is nothing I should boast about except one thing, and that is that I know Jesus Christ, who gave His blood and bore everything for me, and who came so that I might have life abundantly. I had always been listening to the words of the thief. When I started listening to my saviour instead, I forgot everything else and started writing about Him alone.
Being discouraged
5Talents: As a young leader, have you had people discourage you? How do you handle it?

Many times my heart and my soul fail to manage a difficult situation, and God gives me the strength to manage it in some other way. I follow the rule in Matthew 18 — go and speak to the person directly first, and if they will not listen, take one or two others with you.

I was a great sinner and I did many things that people could find to gossip about. Whenever I face that kind of situation I remember one thing: that the Lord Jesus came for sinners, not for the righteous. Though I have been a sinner since birth, I trust God, and His power makes me clean every day.
5Talents: What would you say to someone who is talented but sad, because they have not been given an opportunity, or their talent is not recognised?

Everything has its own time according to God's will. A worshipper should worship and praise Him at all times, and it does not matter where they are — wherever they are breathing, they should worship. Psalm 37:4 says, be glad in God and He will give you the desires of your heart. So we should begin by being glad in God, and He will give us the opportunities in the proper way.

articles.title: Two things you can say when you wake up, and they decide the rest of the day
articles.deck: “Good Lord, it's morning” or “Good morning, Lord.” Lorita Das on gratitude, on the exercise of imagining you have lost everything, and on why humility is not the same as being a doormat.

archiveMeta.editNote: Lightly edited for reading order and typographical errors.

body.v: “If the only prayer you said was ‘thank you’, that would be enough.” — Meister Eckhart

When we wake up in the morning there are two possible expressions, and one of them is going to govern the day. Either the overwhelmed gasp — “Good Lord, it's morning” — or the shout of joy: “Good morning, Lord.”

If we fall into the first category, and I am fairly sure most of us do, we push ourselves through the day complaining about the world's problems and behaving as though every burden had landed on our shoulders. If we fall into the second, we start on a grateful note and move through the day calmly, noticing and appreciating what the Lord has given.
The exercise

As Christians we should carry an attitude of gratitude: counting blessings, noticing small pleasures, acknowledging everything we receive. Most of the time we focus on what we lack instead of what we have, and take for granted the good things already in our lives. We complain about the house not being big enough, or the clothes, or the pay. We wish we could do things differently.

For those of us who think like that, there is a gratitude exercise. Imagine losing some of the things you take for granted — your family, your friends, your ability to see or hear, anything that currently gives you comfort. Then imagine getting each of them back, one at a time, and consider how grateful you would be for each one.
The other half of it
There is a second virtue that goes hand in hand with gratitude. Proverbs 27:2 says, “Let another praise you, and not your own mouth; someone else and not your own lips.”

God detests pride because it is the sin of putting ourselves in God's place. In this era of marketing we cannot resist the urge to promote ourselves and blow our own trumpets. We make idols of ourselves and become self-important.

The only thing that removes ego is humility, which is simply personal modesty. Humble people are not spineless, and they are not doormats, whatever else is said about them. They are people with their feet firmly on the ground who have put God ahead of themselves. Sometimes our own achievements blind us to the fact that it is the Lord who made us what we are and gave us what we have.
The fullest and best ears of corn hang lowest toward the ground.
Take a moment each day and make a list of five things to thank God for. Do not let it become a formality. Acknowledge His gifts, and thank Him properly for the blessings He keeps giving you.

articles.title: A shoemaker who taught himself six languages, and spent seven years in India without a single convert
articles.deck: William Carey was apprenticed indoors because sunlight blistered his skin. He made a globe out of scrap leather, and did not stop for forty-one years. “I can plod,” he said, when asked to account for himself.

archiveMeta.editNote: The 2012 version of this piece was not original work and has been replaced. This is a new article, written from the nineteenth-century biographies and Carey's own Enquiry, listed at the foot.

body.v: This piece first ran in our January 2013 issue. That version was not our own writing and has been replaced. What follows is new work, researched from Carey's own writing and from the nineteenth-century biographies. Sources are listed at the end.
He was put to shoemaking because he could not work outside. Sunlight blistered his skin, so a boy from a weaver's family in Northamptonshire was apprenticed to an indoor trade and sat at a bench.

He kept a book open on that bench. By twenty-one he had taught himself Latin, Greek, Hebrew and Italian, and was starting on Dutch and French. He made a globe of the world out of scraps of leather, and marked on it what he could find out about every country: the size, the population, what people believed there.
Somebody called that cottage Carey's College. It was a cobbler's front room.
Paulerspury
William Carey was born on 17 August 1761 in a thatched cottage in Paulerspury, an ordinary Northamptonshire village. His family were weavers and he was not sent to be educated.

At around eighteen he left the Church of England, joined the Congregational church at Hackleton where he was apprenticed, and married there in 1781. He began walking the five miles to Olney and back looking for people who would argue theology with him. Olney was a stronghold of the Particular Baptists, and he was baptised among them in October 1783. Two years later he moved to Moulton to be a schoolmaster, and a year after that became the pastor of its small Baptist congregation.
He was, at this point, a village pastor with no money, no standing and no formal education, who could read six languages.
A book about a sea voyage
What set him off was not a sermon. It was a travel book.
My attention to missions was first awakened after I was at Moulton, by reading the Last Voyage of Captain Cook.
body.highlight: by reading the Last Voyage of Captain Cook

body.v: Most readers took Cook's journals as adventure. Carey read them as a population census. He started reading everything he could find that bore on the subject, making notes, filling in the leather globe.

When he raised the question at a ministers' meeting — whether the command to teach all nations still bound ministers now — an older man told him to sit down, and that when God chose to reach the nations He would do it without Carey's help. He did not sit down. In 1792 he published An Enquiry Into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens, which surveyed the history of missions, then went country by country through the known world with the size, the population and the religion of each, and then dealt with the practical question of how any of it could actually be done.
It is an odd document to read now. Half sermon, half spreadsheet. The spreadsheet half is why it worked.

That May he preached at Nottingham on what became the sentence he is remembered for: expect great things from God, attempt great things for God. The Baptist Missionary Society was founded at Kettering that October. Carey had no money to put into the subscription and pledged the profits from his book instead.
Serampore
He sailed in 1793. His wife Dorothy did not want to go, and after two returns from the docks to persuade her, she and the children came.

The East India Company would not have missionaries in its territory, so the work ended up at Serampore, a small Danish colony on the Hooghly north of Calcutta, where the Danish governor would have them and the Company could not reach them. The whole enterprise ran for years out of a foreign enclave fifteen miles from British power.

What they built there was a printing house. Carey learned the languages, ran the presses, and by the time he died the Scriptures had been translated and printed in around forty languages and dialects — Bengali, Sanskrit, Marathi, Assamese, Oriya and on down the list. He wrote grammars and dictionaries for languages that had never had one. He printed the first prose books in Bengali, and helped start the first Bengali newspaper. He taught at Fort William College, and in 1818 he and his colleagues founded Serampore College, which was chartered by Denmark to grant degrees and admitted students regardless of caste or religion. It is still open.

He was also, seriously and not as a hobby, a botanist. He kept a five-acre garden at Serampore, corresponded with Kew, published on Indian flora and in 1820 founded the Agri-Horticultural Society of India, arguing that better agriculture was a straightforwardly good thing to give a country. A genus of flowering plant is named after him.

And he campaigned for years against sati, the burning of widows on their husbands' funeral pyres. He collected the evidence and kept putting it in front of the administration. When the practice was finally prohibited in 1829, the edict was handed to him on a Sunday morning to be translated into Bengali. He gave up preaching that day and translated it immediately, so that it could take effect without losing a week.
What it cost
Seven years passed in India before a single Indian person came to faith through their work. Seven years is a very long time to be wrong in public.

In March 1812 the Serampore printing house burned down. It took the presses, the type for a dozen languages, the paper, and the manuscripts — years of translation, including a polyglot dictionary he had been compiling. Work that could not be reconstructed from anything. He began again.

The hardest part of the account is his family. A five-year-old son, Peter, died of dysentery early on. Dorothy — who had not wanted to come, who lost a child in a country she had no wish to be in — became severely mentally ill and remained so for about twelve years until her death in 1807. She is a real cost of this story and she did not choose it. Any honest telling of Carey has to sit with that rather than move past it, and most tellings do move past it.
Why he is still known

He is called the father of modern missions, which is a title that flattens him. What he actually was is a translator, a printer, a lexicographer, a botanist and a college founder, who worked in one place for forty-one years and never once went home on leave.
He died at Serampore on 9 June 1834, aged seventy-two. He had asked that a friend not talk about Dr Carey after he was gone, but about Dr Carey's God.
So what, in 2026?
Somebody once asked what accounted for what he had done. His answer was two words: “I can plod.”

That is a strange thing to read now. Everything around you is built to suggest that the way things happen is fast — that you find the thing, it takes off, and if it does not take off in a reasonable time you were wrong about it. Seven years of no result is not a season anyone plans for.

Carey had seven of them, then a fire that took the work back to nothing, and then he did it again. He was not unusually gifted at any single thing except staying. If you are trying to work out whether to keep going with something slow, he is not an inspiring story so much as a plain piece of evidence: the compounding is real, and almost nobody is around long enough to collect it.

Sources: William Carey, An Enquiry Into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens (1792); Eustace Carey, Memoir of William Carey (1836); George Smith, The Life of William Carey, Shoemaker and Missionary (1885), at the Christian Classics Ethereal Library; S. Pearce Carey, William Carey (1923); and the records of Serampore College and of the Agri-Horticultural Society of India.
